children: India’s burgeoning gold loan market is increasingly seen in a light beyond that of secured lending. At its most basic, a gold loan represents a way for households to raise cash against an asset without liquidating it and has implications for financial inclusion for those who might not otherwise have ready access to formal forms of credit.

Gold holds a special place in the Indian household. It is pervasive across income levels and geographies and can be a viable source of collateral. Unlike unsecured borrowing which can sometimes be fraught with issues pertaining to creditworthiness, income proofing and other such considerations, gold as collateral is a secured debt product. This can be an alternate avenue for both individuals and businesses to tap into the credit market.

The rise in gold loans also reflects a shift in borrower behavior. Gold loans are no longer viewed as something that only local moneylenders would offer but rather as a part of the wider financial system. By bringing gold lending into the formal financial system through entities like NBFC, organized lending will lead to better documentation and regulation of this segment that has existed in India for centuries.

This can be of particular interest in emerging cities and other underserved markets. Borrowers in such locations may have limited access to an extensive array of products at their disposal, despite having valuable assets. In such cases, expansion of the formal gold loan network will help to bring secured credit closer to such customers, and reduce their reliance on informal sources of financing.

Technology has a crucial role to play in enabling this expansion to be scaled. By introducing digital onboarding, centralised processes and data led underwriting and technology enabled customer service, lenders stand to benefit from being able to serve customers more efficiently across a wider geographic footprint. The use of digital tools can also make information around loan terms, repayment schedules and servicing more accessible to customers, supporting a more informed borrowing experience.

The opportunity goes beyond just geography. Gold loans can cater to different financial needs including short term household needs as well as business working capital and other liquidity requirements. Especially for people in small businesses and the self-employed, where cash flow needs may not match with the loan process, access to secured credit could be very relevant.

Co-lending can also catalyse this eco-system with its ability to combine the outreach of multiple lenders with differentiated expertise, customer knowledge and capital resources. Co-lending models can also be leveraged to scale formal credit access by building on the combination of differentiated capital and operational capabilities and, if designed with appropriate process and customer safety mechanisms, would bring the discipline of secured lending at a larger scale.

However, financial inclusion should not be measured only on the amount of loans disbursed, but the responsible lending, transparent communication, appropriate assessment of collateral and full understanding of the obligations related to accessing a loan must be borne in mind. The objective should be to create a situation where people who have greater access to credit would also receive greater financial assistance, rather than the opposite.

India’s gold loan boom is a structural opportunity. It is an indication of how an asset deeply entrenched in the country’s household wealth can act as an enabler to access other financial services. As organised lenders grow their presence, technology makes distribution easier and new lending models emerge, gold-backed credit has the potential to penetrate deeper into the customer base, reaching out to those who have so far been on the periphery of the formal credit system.

The story of India’s gold loan market growth is not one simply of precious metal. It is a tale of a way to tap into the existing deep pool of gold holdings in Indian homes, in order to extend credit to more families. And that makes India’s continuing push to liberalize gold lending a notable part of its long-standing journey to promote inclusion in finance.

title: Why India’s gold loan boom is becoming a story about financial inclusion
